argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0103b: meeting "b" (functional design) of series SY0103.

PROJECT
The team is designing a voice-controlled kitchen timer.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Project Manager (PM)  Laura  present
B  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomasz  ABSENT, never speaks
C  User Interface designer (UI)  Priya  present
D  Marketing Expert (ME)  Ben  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0103a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kick-off meeting, the team members introduced themselves and their roles, and the project manager introduced the project: a voice-controlled kitchen timer that people can use when their hands are dirty from cooking. The project manager presented the financial targets: a selling price of 25 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit and an overall profit target of 15 million euros. On the budget, the industrial designer estimated a simple command-recognition chip at three to four euros and raised the open question of battery versus mains power, since always listening for a wake word drains batteries and a mains adapter adds cost. The marketing expert's idea of a recipe screen with wifi was judged not to fit the budget. On voice interaction, the team agreed that speech recognition should run on the device with a small fixed set of commands rather than through a phone app. It should use a wake word, probably a distinctive product name. It should give short spoken confirmations, and one physical button should serve as a backup for stopping the alarm. Support for multiple named timers was raised as a mainly software feature to explore, and individual research tasks were assigned before the functional design meeting.
  decisions: The target selling price is 25 euros and production cost must not exceed 12.50 euros per unit. Speech recognition will run on the device itself with a small fixed command set (e.g. set, stop, how long left), not via a phone app. The timer will use a wake word, probably a distinctive name rather than a common word like 'timer'. The timer will have one physical button as a backup, mainly for stopping the alarm. The timer will give short spoken confirmations of commands. A recipe screen with wifi is out of scope because it does not fit the budget.
  actions: The industrial designer will research the components (speech chip, microphone, speaker) and the power question, and produce a rough cost breakdown against the 12.50 euro limit. The user interface designer will work out the voice interaction: wake word, command list, spoken feedback and multiple timers. The marketing expert will research what users want from kitchen timers, what they complain about, and whether customers will pay 25 euros for a timer. The marketing expert will come up with candidate names for the wake word. The project manager will write up the minutes and send them to the team.
  problems: Whether the timer will run on batteries or mains power is still open, because always-on listening drains batteries while a mains adapter adds cost and a cable. It is not yet known whether all components fit within 12.50 euros. The marketing expert questioned whether customers will pay 25 euros when ordinary kitchen timers cost around five euros. Support for multiple simultaneous timers was raised but not yet decided.
  action item SY0103a.ai1: Research components (speech chip, microphone, speaker) and power options, and produce a rough cost breakdown against the 12.50 euro limit (owner B, active)
  action item SY0103a.ai2: Work out the voice interaction: wake word, command list, spoken feedback and multiple timers (owner C, active)
  action item SY0103a.ai3: Research user needs and complaints about kitchen timers and whether customers will pay 25 euros (owner D, active)
  action item SY0103a.ai4: Come up with candidate names for the wake word (owner D, active)
  action item SY0103a.ai5: Write up the meeting minutes and send them to the team (owner A, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested using the user's phone for speech recognition so the timer would just be a speaker; this was not adopted.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested a screen with recipe suggestions and wifi; the project manager judged it would not fit the budget.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer suggested 'timer' as the wake word; it was rejected because it is a common word that would trigger by accident.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_PLAN_CHANGE [F1]: The team agrees on a plan early in the meeting, then later in the same meeting changes it (different choice, date, or approach). The gold summary must state only the FINAL plan, and may mention that it was revised.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_ABSENT_DISCUSSED [F1]: One team member is absent. The others discuss them (why they are away, what they would think, what to tell them). The absent person never speaks. The gold summary must not attribute any statement to the absent person.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
